Berdychiv Old Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Zhytomyrska oblast, Ukraine

Demolished. This final record closes an extraordinary collection: Berdychiv's Old Jewish cemetery, likely dating to as early as the 16th or 17th century, though its earliest confirmed tombstone — that of Rabbi Eliezer Lieber the Great, who died around 1770 — dates to 1771. Berdychiv's Jews, first mentioned in 1593, transformed the town into a major commercial and religious center, earning it the nickname 'Jerusalem of Volhynia'; the community grew from 1,220 in 1765 to 41,617 (78 percent) by 1897. In the late 18th century, Berdychiv attracted the beloved Hasidic master Rabbi Levi Yitzchok (1740–1809), one of the most cherished figures in Hasidic tradition, renowned for his passionate love of the Jewish people. The town became a major center of Haskalah in the 19th century and one of the most important hubs of Jewish printing in the Russian Empire, with its first press established in 1798. Berdychiv was the birthplace of an extraordinary array of cultural figures: brothers Anton (1829–1894) and Nikolai Rubinstein (1835–1881), founders of the St. Petersburg and Moscow Conservatories respectively; the legendary pianist Vladimir Horowitz (1903–1989), among the greatest of the 20th century; Yiddish writer Der Nister (Pinchus Kahanovich, 1884–1950); and novelist and war correspondent Vasily Grossman (1905–1964), author of the monumental Holocaust chronicle 'Life and Fate.' By 1907, the community maintained six synagogues, 72 prayer houses, two Jewish cemeteries, a hospital, an orphanage, and numerous schools and libraries; Ukraine's first Yiddish-language law court (1924) and Jewish police commissariat (1926) were both established here. Following the German occupation of July 1941, 38,366 local and refugee Jews were murdered in Berdychiv between 1941 and 1944. This cemetery fell into disuse by the 19th century; 1929 excavations aimed at conservation were instead followed by its 1932 demolition to build a park, which the Germans later used as a war cemetery during the occupation, itself demolished immediately after liberation. A replica tombstone for Rabbi Eliezer Lieber the Great was erected in the 1980s near his original grave site, close to the park's entrance.
